source.title: MemoNet: Memorizing All Cross Features' Representations Efficiently via Multi-Hash Codebook Network for CTR Prediction

record.tranche_reason: The paper is inspired by language-model scaling and proposes a CTR model with a codebook-size scaling sweep, but it does not test the claim’s language-model loss laws or fit a power law.
record.gate_note: The study reports CTR AUC trends as HCNet codebook size changes. These are findings about scaling a CTR model, not held-out language-model cross-entropy, power-law fits, or the claim’s compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. It also discusses language-model scaling in its motivation; cited language-model results are not rows.
record.test_reason: A CTR recommendation-model paper. It borrows the term 'scaling law' and sweeps its own codebook size, but reports only AUC trends from a figure. It fits no power law and measures no held-out loss against parameters, data or compute, so it cannot show whether any version's power-law form holds. The sweep is a performance analysis of the authors' own method, not a test of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The authors conclude that MemoNet beats state-of-the-art CTR models. They also claim it 'shows scaling law of large language model': enlarging the codebook sustainably raises AUC on Avazu and Criteo up to 100M codewords, while KDD12 peaks at 0.5M. The record's addition that no power law is fitted is a fact about the paper, not part of the authors' conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: A CTR prediction model with a multi-hash codebook and DNN backbone; it scales codeword count and measures CTR metrics rather than language-model pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported codebook-size trend differs by dataset: Avazu and Criteo continue improving through the tested maximum, whereas KDD12 has a stated optimum at 0.5M codewords.

fits_no_version.finding: CTR AUC rises with HCNet codebook size up to 100M codewords on Avazu and Criteo, but peaks at 0.5M on KDD12. Separately, the authors say deepening the DNN backbone gives only 0.1-0.2 AUC.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Enlarging an embedding or memory table in CTR models gives sustained but dataset-dependent gains, unlike scaling dense CTR model parameters. No power-law form is shown.

record.peer_reviewed: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM ’23)
record.problems: The scaling sweep’s plotted values are not fully available in the text; only qualitative trends and selected endpoint or optimum statements are described. The authors report averaged results from five random seeds for the main model comparisons, but no uncertainty estimates for the scaling sweep. No power-law fit is reported.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-sweep rows were left out.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Whether a power-law form holds in CTR or recommendation. Only qualitative AUC gains with codebook size are shown.
Downstream predictability from scale or loss.
Dependence of exponents or fits on setup or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: Table 2 also gives test logloss for 1M versus 10M codewords, for example Avazu MemoNet-L 0.3704 to 0.3684. These are two points from the authors' own method comparison, so they do not establish a power-law relation and are not added as rows. The reader's T4/uses_without_test is changed to discusses/T6: the scaling law serves as motivation and framing, not as a tool.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law form and range.
No small-run power-law fit or prediction of much larger language-model runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between model parameters and training tokens.
No comparison of language-model architecture shapes at fixed parameter count.
The paper scales a CTR codebook but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in this or another regime.
No downstream language-model task performance or relation to pretraining loss.
No comparison of power-law fitting choices, exponents, or compute-optimal splits.

rows.subject: MemoNet-L and MemoNet-A (reported together; results not disaggregated in the text)
rows.size_stated: Codebook size increased from 0.01M to 100M; at 100M the codebook contains 100M codewords.
rows.operation_detail: Increased HCNet codeword count while evaluating CTR performance.
rows.value: Both models’ performance continues to increase; at 100M codewords, AUC is 79.91% (model not specified).
rows.note: The text describes the trend and gives the endpoint AUC, but does not attribute that endpoint to MemoNet-L or MemoNet-A. No power-law fit is reported.
rows.check: Measure is CTR AUC versus codebook size, a monotone trend with no power-law fit. It cannot bear on V1 or V5's power-law form. The 79.91% endpoint is not attributed to a variant.

rows.subject: MemoNet-L and MemoNet-A (reported together; results not disaggregated in the text)
rows.size_stated: Codebook sizes are varied; the stated optimal codeword count is 0.5M.
rows.operation_detail: Varied HCNet codeword count while evaluating CTR performance.
rows.measure: CTR performance; specific metric for the stated optimum not specified in the text
rows.value: The optimal codeword number is 0.5M; the text attributes this to fewer useful cross features in the dataset.
rows.note: The text states the optimum but does not give its metric value or distinguish the two MemoNet variants. This does not establish a power law.
rows.check: Only a stated optimum at 0.5M codewords, with no metric value. Gains stop beyond the optimum, but no fit is given.
